subject: physics

items.q: A sheet of glass transmits almost all of the visible light that reaches it, but absorbs much of the ultraviolet. What does this show?
items.correct: Whether a substance absorbs or transmits a wave can depend on the wavelength of that wave.
items.misconception: A material that looks clear must transmit every electromagnetic wave that reaches it.
items.why: Everyday judgements about materials are made with the eye, which senses only one narrow band of wavelengths, so 'transparent' feels like a whole-material property. Transparency belongs to a material and a wavelength together. Glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet reaching it, while a brick wall stops visible light but transmits radio waves.
items.random_wrong: Ultraviolet is absorbed by every substance it meets, whatever that substance is.

items.q: A mobile phone signal (radio waves) passes through the brick wall of a house, but visible light from outside does not. Which statement explains this best?
items.correct: One substance can transmit one wavelength while absorbing or reflecting another.
items.misconception: Radio waves are absorbed by every material, so brick makes no difference to them.
items.why: Waves are learned as a list of named types with fixed properties and uses, which invites students to attach behaviour to the wave and forget the material it meets. It takes both. The specification states that different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength — the substance and the wavelength together decide what happens.
items.random_wrong: Brick reflects radio waves back outside, and the phone detects those reflected waves.

items.q: Which statement about substances and electromagnetic waves matches the specification?
items.correct: Substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves in ways varying with wavelength.
items.misconception: A given substance treats all wavelengths of electromagnetic wave in the same way.
items.why: Everyday judgements about materials are made with the eye, which senses only one narrow band of wavelengths, so 'transparent' feels like a whole-material property. Transparency belongs to a material and a wavelength together. Glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet reaching it, while a brick wall stops visible light but transmits radio waves.
items.random_wrong: Absorption is decided by the wave alone, so the substance it meets is irrelevant.

items.q: Refraction of an electromagnetic wave at a boundary between two substances is due to which of the following?
items.correct: The difference in the velocity of the wave in the two substances either side of it.
items.misconception: The wave bouncing off the boundary between the two substances at an angle.
items.why: Refraction is taught as a bending of light long before the wave picture is available, so students remember the shape of the diagram and invent a mechanical cause for it. Nothing in the ray diagram itself shows a change of speed. Refraction happens because the velocity of the wave differs in the two substances. If a wave travelled at the same velocity in both, it would cross the boundary without changing direction, however steeply it met the boundary.
items.random_wrong: The difference in the frequency of the wave in the two substances either side of it.

items.q: A wave crosses at an angle into a second substance in which it travels at exactly the same velocity as in the first. What happens at the boundary?
items.correct: It carries on in the same direction, as there is no difference in velocity to refract it.
items.misconception: It bends towards the normal, because a ray entering any new substance bends that way.
items.why: Almost every worked example met first is air into glass, so students learn one arrow direction and treat it as the rule for all boundaries rather than as one case of it. The direction of bending depends on which way the wave crosses the boundary. Entering glass or water from air it bends towards the normal; leaving glass or water into air it bends away from the normal.
items.random_wrong: It bends away from the normal, because the second substance is a different material.

items.q: A ray of light travels through air and meets a glass block at an angle of incidence of 40°. In a correct ray diagram, the refracted ray inside the glass is drawn:
items.correct: bent towards the normal, at an angle of refraction smaller than 40° from the normal.
items.misconception: bent away from the normal, at an angle of refraction larger than 40° from the normal.
items.why: Almost every worked example met first is air into glass, so students learn one arrow direction and treat it as the rule for all boundaries rather than as one case of it. The direction of bending depends on which way the wave crosses the boundary. Entering glass or water from air it bends towards the normal; leaving glass or water into air it bends away from the normal.
items.random_wrong: bent towards the normal, at an angle of refraction measured as 40° from the boundary.

items.q: A ray of light inside a glass block reaches the far surface at an angle of incidence of 25° and passes out into the air. In the ray diagram the emerging ray is:
items.correct: bent away from the normal, so the angle from the normal is greater than 25°.
items.misconception: bent towards the normal, because refraction always turns a ray towards the normal.
items.why: Almost every worked example met first is air into glass, so students learn one arrow direction and treat it as the rule for all boundaries rather than as one case of it. The direction of bending depends on which way the wave crosses the boundary. Entering glass or water from air it bends towards the normal; leaving glass or water into air it bends away from the normal.
items.random_wrong: bent away from the boundary, so the angle from the boundary is greater than 25°.

items.q: A ray of light travelling through air meets the flat surface of a water tank along the normal. How should the ray diagram be drawn?
items.correct: The ray is drawn continuing straight on into the water without changing direction.
items.misconception: The ray is drawn bending slightly towards the normal as it enters the water.
items.why: Students learn 'refraction happens at a boundary' as an unconditional rule and apply it to the one case where the geometry gives no change of direction. At an angle of incidence of zero there is no change of direction, so the ray is drawn as a straight line through the boundary. On the Higher tier, note that the wave still changes speed — it simply has no sideways effect to produce.
items.random_wrong: The ray is drawn bending away from the normal as it enters the water.

items.q: Which line must be added to a refraction ray diagram before the angles of incidence and refraction can be marked on it?
items.correct: A dashed line at right angles to the boundary where the incident ray meets it.
items.misconception: A dashed line along the boundary itself, from which both angles are measured.
items.why: The boundary is a real drawn line and the normal is only a construction line, so the eye is drawn to the boundary. Both angles then come out as the complement of the correct value. All angles in a ray diagram are measured between a ray and the normal. A diagram must show the normal as a dashed line at 90° to the boundary, with the angles marked from it.
items.random_wrong: A dashed line at right angles to the incident ray at the point it meets the boundary.

items.q: A wave front diagram shows water waves crossing at an angle into a region where they travel more slowly. Why does the direction of travel change?
items.correct: The end of each wave front that crosses first slows first, so the front is turned round.
items.misconception: The frequency of the wave falls in the new region, which turns each wave front round.
items.why: Closer fronts look like a more rapid wave, and students link spacing to frequency rather than to wavelength. The source, not the medium, is what fixes the frequency. The frequency is set by the source and does not change at the boundary. The speed changes, so from v = fλ the wavelength changes with it, and that is what the changed spacing of the wave fronts shows.
items.random_wrong: The wave fronts point along the direction of travel and are dragged round by the boundary.

items.q: In a wave front diagram, a wave passes from a medium where it travels quickly into one where it travels slowly. The wave fronts in the slower medium are drawn:
items.correct: closer together than before, because the wave travels less far in each cycle.
items.misconception: closer together than before, because the frequency of the wave has been reduced.
items.why: Closer fronts look like a more rapid wave, and students link spacing to frequency rather than to wavelength. The source, not the medium, is what fixes the frequency. The frequency is set by the source and does not change at the boundary. The speed changes, so from v = fλ the wavelength changes with it, and that is what the changed spacing of the wave fronts shows.
items.random_wrong: further apart than before, because the wave takes longer to complete each cycle.

items.q: A Leslie cube is filled with hot water and an infrared detector is held the same distance from each face in turn. Which face gives the highest reading?
items.correct: The matt black face, because good absorbers of infrared are also good emitters.
items.misconception: The shiny silver face, because it releases the radiation instead of holding onto it.
items.why: Absorbing and emitting sound like opposites, so students expect a surface that is good at one to be poor at the other, and 'black absorbs everything' is learned first. The same property of the surface governs both. A matt black surface is the best absorber and the best emitter; a shiny silver surface is the poorest absorber and the poorest emitter.
items.random_wrong: Every face reads the same, because the colour of a surface only affects visible light.

items.q: Two identical metal plates, one matt black and one shiny silver, are placed the same distance from a radiant heater for ten minutes. What is found?
items.correct: The matt black plate rises to the higher temperature, as it absorbs more infrared.
items.misconception: The shiny silver plate rises to the higher temperature, as it holds in more infrared.
items.why: Absorbing and emitting sound like opposites, so students expect a surface that is good at one to be poor at the other, and 'black absorbs everything' is learned first. The same property of the surface governs both. A matt black surface is the best absorber and the best emitter; a shiny silver surface is the poorest absorber and the poorest emitter.
items.random_wrong: Both plates rise to the same temperature, as the surface finish affects only light.

items.q: A student compares the faces of a Leslie cube but holds the detector 5 cm from one face and 15 cm from the next. Why are the results not valid?
items.correct: Distance has changed as well as the surface, so the difference cannot be attributed to the surface.
items.misconception: The water cools during the experiment, which is the only variable that has changed.
items.why: Students memorise a stock list of criticisms for practical work and offer one of them instead of checking which variable was actually allowed to change. Cooling is a genuine limitation, and is why the faces should be tested quickly, but here the specific fault is that distance changed alongside the surface, so two variables changed at once.
items.random_wrong: The detector gives readings in the wrong units when it is moved between the faces.

items.q: Does the colour and finish of a surface matter for infrared radiation?
items.correct: Yes. How much infrared a surface absorbs, emits or reflects depends on the nature of that surface.
items.misconception: Black and silver only look different to our eyes, so surface colour can only affect visible light, not infrared.
items.why: Colour is defined for students by vision, and infrared is invisible, so the two seem to belong to separate worlds. Infrared is absorbed, emitted and reflected at a surface just as light is, and the readings in this practical show matt dark surfaces and shiny light surfaces behaving quite differently.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What must be kept the same when comparing the faces of a Leslie cube?
items.correct: The distance from the detector, the position and height of the detector, the timing, and the temperature of the water.
items.misconception: As long as each face is tested with the same detector, the readings can be compared however the detector is placed.
items.why: Students treat 'same equipment' as the whole of a fair test and overlook that the intensity of the radiation received falls off sharply with distance from the surface. Only the nature of the surface may change. Move the detector nearer to one face and its reading rises whatever that face is like, so the comparison no longer tests the surface at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How are wave fronts drawn in relation to the direction of travel?
items.correct: At right angles to the direction of travel, one wavelength apart, each front joining points at the same point in their cycle.
items.misconception: Wave fronts are just rays under another name, so they are drawn along the direction the wave is going.
items.why: Both are lines on a wave diagram and both are introduced as ways of representing the same wave, so the perpendicular relationship between them is easily lost. A ray points along the direction of travel; a wave front lies across it, at 90° to it. That is why turning the fronts at a boundary turns the direction of travel.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the wavelength of a wave change when it enters a different medium?
items.correct: Yes. The speed changes and the frequency does not, so the wavelength changes with the speed and the wave fronts are drawn at a new spacing.
items.misconception: Wavelength belongs to the wave itself, so it stays the same whatever medium the wave is in; only the speed can change.
items.why: Waves are first met as a fixed shape with a labelled wavelength, so wavelength feels like an identity tag for the wave rather than a quantity tied to the speed in the medium. Only the frequency is fixed by the source. With v = fλ, a change of speed at the boundary forces a change of wavelength, which is exactly what the changed spacing of the wave fronts shows.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.6.2.2 Properties of electromagnetic waves 1
